results.title: Club families of countable sets
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: Let $X$ be a set. A family $C$ of subsets of $X$ is club in the countable subsets of $X$ when every member of $C$ is countable (finite or countably infinite), every countable set $x \subseteq X$ is contained in some member of $C$, and for every sequence $x_0 \subseteq x_1 \subseteq x_2 \subseteq \cdots$ of members of $C$ the union $\bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} x_n$ belongs to $C$.

results.title: Stationary families of countable sets
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $X$ be a set. A family $S$ of subsets of $X$ is stationary in the countable subsets of $X$ when $S$ meets every family $C$ that is club in the countable subsets of $X$, that is, some set belongs to both $S$ and $C$.

results.title: Closure points of a finitary function
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $X$ be a set and let $F$ be a function assigning an element of $X$ to every finite subset of $X$. The closure points of $F$ are the countable (finite or countably infinite) sets $a \subseteq X$ such that $F(s) \in a$ for every finite set $s \subseteq a$.

results.title: Closure points of a sequence of finitary functions
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $X$ be a set and let $(F_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of functions, each assigning an element of $X$ to every finite subset of $X$. The closure points of $(F_n)$ are the countable (finite or countably infinite) sets $x \subseteq X$ such that $F_n(s) \in x$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and every finite set $s \subseteq x$.

results.title: Claim of Kourovka Problem 16.62
results.caption: Definition

results.title: Groups whose automorphisms all preserve conjugacy classes can have outer automorphisms
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The claim of Kourovka Problem 16.62 is false: there is a group $G$ such that every automorphism of $G$ sends each element $g \in G$ to a conjugate of $g$, but some automorphism of $G$ is not inner, that is, not of the form $x \mapsto h x h^{-1}$ for any $h \in G$.

results.title: Class-preserving automorphisms need not be inner

results.title: Parameters of a Lucas sequence
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: Lucas sequence parameters are a pair of integers $(P, Q)$ with $Q \ne 0$.

results.title: Coprime Lucas sequence parameters
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Lucas sequence parameters $(P, Q)$ are coprime when there exist integers $x$ and $y$ with $xP + yQ = 1$.

results.title: Lucas sequence $U(P, Q)$
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For Lucas sequence parameters $(P, Q)$, the Lucas sequence $U(P, Q)$ is the integer sequence $(U_n)_{n \ge 0}$ with $U_0 = 0$, $U_1 = 1$ and $U_{n+2} = P U_{n+1} - Q U_n$ for every natural number $n$.

results.title: Companion Lucas sequence $V(P, Q)$
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For Lucas sequence parameters $(P, Q)$, the companion Lucas sequence $V(P, Q)$ is the integer sequence $(V_n)_{n \ge 0}$ with $V_0 = 2$, $V_1 = P$ and $V_{n+2} = P V_{n+1} - Q V_n$ for every natural number $n$.

results.title: Fibonacci parameters for Lucas sequences
results.caption: Definition

results.title: Lucas numbers
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The Lucas numbers are the natural numbers $L_n$ defined by $L_0 = 2$, $L_1 = 1$ and $L_{n+2} = L_{n+1} + L_n$ for every natural number $n$. They begin $2, 1, 3, 4, 7, \dots$.

results.title: The Lucas sequence $U(1, -1)$ is the Fibonacci sequence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n$, the $n$-th term of the Lucas sequence $U(1, -1)$ equals the Fibonacci number $F_n$, where $F_0 = 0$, $F_1 = 1$ and $F_{n+2} = F_{n+1} + F_n$.

results.title: Special primes of a Lucas pair
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For integers $P$ and $Q$, a natural number $p$ is a special prime for the Lucas parameters $(P, Q)$ if $p$ is prime and $p$ divides $\gcd(P, Q)$.

results.title: Lucas sequence of the first kind
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For integers $P$ and $Q$, a sequence of integers $(u_n)_{n \ge 0}$ is the Lucas sequence of the first kind with parameters $P$ and $Q$ when $u_0 = 0$, $u_1 = 1$, and $u_{n+2} = P u_{n+1} - Q u_n$ for every natural number $n$.

results.title: Lucas sequence of the first kind: value at zero
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $(u_n)_{n \ge 0}$ is the Lucas sequence of the first kind with integer parameters $P$ and $Q$, then $u_0 = 0$.

results.title: Lucas sequence of the first kind: value at one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $(u_n)_{n \ge 0}$ is the Lucas sequence of the first kind with integer parameters $P$ and $Q$, then $u_1 = 1$.

results.title: Lucas sequence of the first kind: the recurrence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $(u_n)_{n \ge 0}$ is the Lucas sequence of the first kind with integer parameters $P$ and $Q$, then $u_{n+2} = P u_{n+1} - Q u_n$ for every natural number $n$.

results.title: Nondegenerate Lucas pair
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A pair of integers $(P, Q)$ is nondegenerate when $Q \ne 0$ and, for all complex numbers $\alpha$ and $\beta$ with $\alpha + \beta = P$ and $\alpha \beta = Q$, the quotient $\alpha / \beta$ is not a root of unity. Such $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the two roots of $x^2 - P x + Q$, in either order.

results.title: Addition formula $2U_{m+n} = U_m V_n + V_m U_n$ for Lucas sequences
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all integers $P$ and $Q$ with $Q \neq 0$ and all natural numbers $m$ and $n$, the Lucas sequences $U_n = U_n(P, Q)$ and $V_n = V_n(P, Q)$ satisfy $2U_{m+n} = U_m V_n + V_m U_n$.

results.title: Primes that are not Sophie Germain primes

results.title: MSTD set
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A finite set $A$ of real numbers is an *MSTD set* (more sums than differences) when its difference set has fewer elements than its sumset: $|A - A| < |A + A|$, where $A + A = \{a + b : a, b \in A\}$ and $A - A = \{a - b : a, b \in A\}$.

results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a real $m \times n$ matrix $A$, the vector discrepancy of $A$ is the infimum, over all families $u_1, \dots, u_n$ of unit vectors in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$, of $\max_{1 \le i \le m} \lVert \sum_{j=1}^{n} A_{ij} u_j \rVert$ (taken to be $0$ when $m = 0$), where $\lVert \cdot \rVert$ is the Euclidean norm; it is an element of $[0, \infty]$.

results.title: The vector discrepancy is attained

results.title: Standard enumeration of the recursively enumerable sets
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $e$ and $n$, $n$ belongs to $W_e$, the $e$-th recursively enumerable set, when the partial recursive function $\varphi_e$ computed by the program with index $e$ in the standard numbering of partial recursive programs is defined at $n$; thus $W_e$ is the domain of $\varphi_e$.

results.title: Productive set
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A set $A$ of natural numbers is productive when there is a partial recursive function $f$ such that for every natural number $e$ with $W_e \subseteq A$, where $W_e$ is the $e$-th recursively enumerable set in the standard enumeration, $f(e)$ is defined, $f(e) \in A$ and $f(e) \notin W_e$.

results.title: Creative set
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A set $A$ of natural numbers is creative when it is recursively enumerable and its complement $\mathbb{N} \setminus A$ is productive.

results.title: Immune set
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A set $A$ of natural numbers is immune when it is infinite and every recursively enumerable set $B \subseteq A$ is finite.

results.title: Simple set
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A set $P$ of natural numbers is simple when it is recursively enumerable and its complement $\{n \mid \neg P(n)\}$ is immune.

results.title: A productive set is not recursively enumerable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: No productive set of natural numbers is recursively enumerable: if it were the $e$-th recursively enumerable set $W_e$, its productive function would produce a member of it outside $W_e$.

results.title: An immune set is not recursively enumerable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: It would be an infinite RE subset of itself.

results.title: A simple set is not computable
results.caption: Theorem

results.title: A simple set is recursively enumerable

results.title: A creative set is not computable
results.caption: Theorem

results.title: Root key of a splay tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The optional root key of a binary tree is undefined (none) for the empty tree, and is the key $k$ for a tree whose root node holds $k$.

results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and write $(k; L, R)$ for the binary tree with root key $k$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$. results.title: Splaying the empty tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every key $x$ of a linearly ordered type, splaying $x$ in the empty binary tree gives the empty tree.

results.title: Splaying preserves the inorder traversal
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every key $x$ and every binary tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type, the inorder traversal of the tree obtained by splaying $x$ in $t$ equals the inorder traversal of $t$. No search-tree ordering of $t$ is assumed.

results.title: Splaying preserves membership
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For keys $x$ and $y$ and a binary tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type, $y$ is a key of the tree obtained by splaying $x$ in $t$ if and only if $y$ is a key of $t$.

results.title: Splaying preserves the number of nodes
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every binary tree $t$ with keys in a linearly ordered type and every key $x$, the tree obtained by splaying $x$ in $t$ has the same number of nodes as $t$.

results.title: Splaying preserves the search-tree property
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys in a linearly ordered type and let $x$ be a key. If $t$ is a binary search tree (at every node, every key of the left subtree is strictly smaller and every key of the right subtree strictly larger than the key of the node), then the tree obtained by splaying $x$ in $t$ is again a binary search tree.

results.title: Splaying a present key brings it to the root
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a binary search tree with keys in a linearly ordered type (at every node, every key of the left subtree is strictly smaller and every key of the right subtree strictly larger than the key of the node), and let $x$ be a key that occurs in $t$. Then there are binary trees $l$ and $r$ such that splaying $x$ in $t$ gives the tree whose root holds $x$, with left subtree $l$ and right subtree $r$.

results.title: Root key after splaying a present key
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a binary search tree with keys in a linearly ordered type (at every node, every key of the left subtree is strictly smaller and every key of the right subtree strictly larger than the key of the node), and let $x$ be a key that occurs in $t$. Then the tree obtained by splaying $x$ in $t$ is nonempty and its root key is $x$.

results.title: Splay-tree split parts contain only original keys
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For keys $x$ and $y$ and a binary tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type, if $y$ is a key of the left part or of the right part of the split of $t$ at $x$, then $y$ is a key of $t$.

results.title: Keys other than the split key survive a split
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys in a linearly ordered type, and let $x$ and $y$ be keys with $y \ne x$. If $y$ occurs as a key of $t$, then $y$ occurs as a key of the left part or of the right part of the split of $t$ at $x$. The tree $t$ need not be a binary search tree.

results.title: Splitting an ordered tree separates the keys around the split key
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be an ordered binary tree over a linearly ordered type and let $x$ be a key. When $t$ is split at $x$, every key of the left part is strictly less than $x$ and every key of the right part is strictly greater than $x$.

results.title: Both parts of a split search tree are search trees
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys in a linearly ordered type and let $x$ be a key. If $t$ is a binary search tree (at every node, every key of the left subtree is strictly smaller and every key of the right subtree strictly larger than the key of the node), then the left part and the right part of the split of $t$ at $x$ are both binary search trees.

results.title: Splay-tree insertion
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a key $x$ and a binary tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type, inserting $x$ into $t$ splays $x$ in $t$, splits the resulting tree at $x$ into a left part and a right part, and returns the tree whose root key is $x$, whose left subtree is the left part and whose right subtree is the right part.

results.title: Splay-tree access
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a key $x$ and a binary tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type, the access of $x$ in $t$ is the pair $(b, t')$, where $t'$ is the tree obtained by splaying $x$ in $t$ and $b$ is true exactly when $t'$ is nonempty and its root key is $x$.

results.title: Splay-tree membership test
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a key $x$ and a binary tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type, the membership test of $x$ in $t$ is the Boolean component of the access of $x$ in $t$: it is true exactly when the tree obtained by splaying $x$ in $t$ is nonempty and its root key is $x$.

results.title: The tree returned by a splay-tree access
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a key $x$ and a binary tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type, the tree component of the access of $x$ in $t$ is the tree obtained by splaying $x$ in $t$.

results.title: Keys after splay-tree insertion
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For keys $x$ and $y$ and a binary tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type, $y$ is a key of the tree obtained by splay-tree insertion of $x$ into $t$ if and only if $y = x$ or $y$ is a key of $t$.

results.title: Splay-tree insertion preserves the search-tree property
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys in a linearly ordered type and let $x$ be a key. If $t$ is a binary search tree (at every node, every key of the left subtree is strictly smaller and every key of the right subtree strictly larger than the key of the node), then the splay-tree insertion of $x$ into $t$ is again a binary search tree.

results.title: Splay-tree insertion puts the inserted key at the root
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every binary tree $t$ with keys in a linearly ordered type and every key $x$, the splay-tree insertion of $x$ into $t$ is a nonempty tree whose root key is $x$.

results.title: Correctness of the splay-tree membership test
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For an ordered binary tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type and a key $x$, the splay-tree membership test of $x$ in $t$ returns true if and only if $x$ is a key of $t$.
